questions.q: In most real-world exposed-storage-bucket incidents, what actually failed?
options: A customer-side access setting (ACL, bucket policy, or container access level) made the bucket publicly reachable
The cloud provider's underlying infrastructure was breached directly
The encryption algorithm used on the data was broken
The provider's network backbone was compromised
questions.explain: In case after case, the provider's infrastructure was never breached — a customer-side setting (a legacy ACL granting access to AllUsers, or a bucket/container set to public and never reverted) made the data reachable by anyone.

questions.q: What does enabling S3 Block Public Access at the account level actually do?
options: It encrypts every object in every bucket in the account automatically
It overrides any ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access, across every current and future bucket in the account
It only affects buckets created after the setting is turned on, not existing ones
It deletes any object that currently has public read permissions
questions.explain: Block Public Access at the account level is deliberately blunt: it overrides ACLs and bucket policies that would grant public access, applying to every bucket in the account including future ones — which is why it's the highest-leverage control against this class of incident.

questions.q: On Azure Storage, which container public access level is the most dangerous, and why?
options: Private, because it silently allows anonymous reads despite its name
Blob, because it allows anonymous write access to the container
Container, because it allows anonymous read of blob data AND container/blob listing, letting anyone enumerate everything inside
There is no meaningful difference between the access levels
questions.explain: The Container access level allows anonymous read of blob data plus listing of the container and blob names, letting anyone enumerate the full contents — more exposure than Blob, which only allows anonymous read of blob data itself.

questions.q: If an Azure storage account has "Allow Blob public access" set to Disabled, what happens if someone sets an individual container's public access level to "Container"?
options: The container becomes publicly readable immediately, overriding the account-level setting
Azure automatically re-enables the account-level setting to match the container
The storage account is automatically deleted for the policy violation
The container-level setting has no effect, because the account-level setting blocks public access for every container regardless of its own setting
questions.explain: The account-level "Allow Blob public access" setting governs whether any container-level public setting can take effect at all. With it disabled, a container's own public access level setting is effectively inert.

questions.q: Why doesn't encrypting a storage object protect against a public-ACL style exposure?
options: Encryption always prevents this; the two problems are actually the same issue

Encryption at rest protects data if it's exfiltrated through a channel other than the normal read path, but a public ACL grants access through the normal read path itself, which decrypts the object for any authorized reader — including the public
Encryption only applies to data in transit, never to data at rest
Public ACLs bypass the storage service entirely, so encryption settings never apply to them
questions.explain: A public ACL or public access setting authorizes normal reads from anyone — the storage service serves the (decrypted, from the reader's perspective) object through its standard read path. Encryption at rest doesn't block that; it protects against channels that bypass normal authorized access.
